blocks.comment:
This work presents a draft genome-scale metabolic reconstruction of Megasphaera sp. MJR8396C and simulates its growth and secretion profile under gut-like conditions and under controlled nutrient formulations. A two-species community model comprising Megasphaera sp. MJR8396C and Bifidobacterium adolescentis was used to investigate potential metabolic interactions between the strains.
The authors have adequately addressed the statements made by the reviewers, both in their response to the reviewers and in the revision of the manuscript. However, I feel that reviewer 2 has a point on the suitability of the “draft” reconstruction in making predictions with biological significance. I see little curation of the reconstruction in the revised version.
blocks.response: We agree that numerical reproducibility and a MEMOTE score alone cannot establish predictive biological validity. The revision now tests biomass mass closure and precursor producibility, maintenance and uptake sensitivity, closed-boundary energy generation, loop-free exchange extrema, global GPR effects and transfer dependence. Original JGI inputs are recovered and all 477 model genes have sequence-supported public-locus mappings. The response below identifies the actual curation and the remaining biochemical evidence gaps; we do not present this draft as an experimentally validated strain-specific reference model.

blocks.comment:
The promising aspects of the work are the choice of the genomes selected for modelling, the problem statement of identifying metabolite secretion and cross-feeding in the gut, transparency in reporting the models’ shortcomings, and the quantum of work carried out. The results presented in the nutrient-dependent growth are interesting. The concurrence of the models’ predictions with certain experimental data is another positive.
The paper does not contain any fundamental flaws that would preclude publication, however, for a manuscript focused on building strain-specific GEMs, merely auditing the reconstruction using MEMOTE is not sufficient. Removal of modelling artefacts like blocked reactions, infeasible cycles, biomass precursor curation are essential, especially when one wants to predict more than just the growth of the organism. The formulation of the biomass equation is another important aspect that must be taken into account. The MEMOTE report does point out that the models are somewhat lacking in that aspect also. Inclusion of a couple of these computational curation steps in addition to improving the GPR will complete the picture. The lack of curation of these artefacts reduces the significance of the work. The disclaimers already presented in the discussion go a long way to mitigate these limitations, nevertheless the standard is not suitable for this journal, without another revision addressing these concerns, not merely adding them to the limitations.
blocks.response: The revision now makes three sequence-supported GPR edits: Bcd plus both Etf subunits, all six Rnf subunits, and inferred full-length PFOR homologs. The original model remains unchanged; the derivative has 483 genes and identical stoichiometry/bounds. Matched biomass, precursor/carrier, ATP and loopless checks, plus inclusion-minimal added-reaction sensitivity, accompany these edits. Unsupported complete pathway or measured-biomass claims remain excluded.

blocks.comment: Line 126: Medium-conditioned GEM is a misleading phrase. It may indicate a growth medium formulation used for the gap filling or simulation.
blocks.response: The phrase has been removed from the current manuscript. We describe a gapseq-derived draft reconstruction gapfilled using the stated anaerobic medium and simulated under explicitly defined nutrient constraints. The Methods also state that using the same medium for gapfilling and simulation makes baseline growth expected by construction.

blocks.comment: Line 207: Why was the genome compared to C. sporogenes? Please justify in the manuscript.
blocks.response: C. sporogenes is retained only as a functional comparator for characterized reductive amino-acid gene-cluster architecture. It is not used as a close phylogenetic comparator. The Methods and Results now state this explicitly; the taxonomic analysis instead uses reciprocal ANI and accession-resolved Megasphaera references.

blocks.comment: In table 2: When similarity percentages are low (I see values like 20% and 33%) query coverage becomes an important aspect in homology detection. Please mention the cut-off used.
blocks.response: The 20%, 33%, 50%, 66% and 100% values are archived gutSMASH KnownClusterBlast fractions of reference-cluster genes with homologs, not pairwise amino-acid identities or query-alignment coverage. Table 2 uses one consistent term, candidate match, and gives the observed reference-gene fraction without treating a universal fraction as proof of an intact pathway. Separately, the new reviewed-reference DIAMOND candidate flag requires at least 30% identity and at least 70% coverage on both query and subject. All alignment values and provisional functional decisions are supplied in S54/S61. The archived gutSMASH invocation does not establish a separate custom per-hit coverage cutoff; none is invented.

blocks.comment: Line 472: A bitscore threshold for pathway and transport searches is not optimal. A query coverage should ideally be enforced.
blocks.response: The recovered gapseq output and pinned source resolve this point more precisely than the earlier response. At recorded commit c64db99b, both pathway and transporter searches default to 75% reference-query coverage and explicitly pass the filter to BLAST/DIAMOND. In the original files, all 20,283 reaction-table rows with recorded coverage and all 10,613 transporter rows have 75-100% coverage; none is below 75%. The Methods now report this evidence alongside the bit-score threshold of 200. Complete historical command-line recovery is not claimed. Reference-query coverage is distinguished from subject coverage and from gutSMASH cluster coverage.

blocks.comment: Line 518: There is a discrepancy in the wording in the revised manuscript and Line 362-363 in the marked-up manuscript. The one in the revised manuscript is apt.
blocks.response: The tracked manuscript is regenerated mechanically from the frozen v4 clean source and the final v5 clean source. Both documents therefore represent the same current wording; their pagination and line numbers naturally differ. The response cites line numbers exported from the compiled clean manuscript rather than carrying forward the old line 518/362-363 references.

blocks.comment: Line 528 - 530: Why were pFBA and FVA carried out? The discussion could include a couple of sentences on the same.
blocks.response: The Discussion now explains why both calculations are needed. pFBA selects a representative minimum-total-flux state after optimizing biomass. It does not establish a unique secretion phenotype. FVA reports the feasible range of each selected exchange under a stated growth requirement; broad nitrogen/sulfur ranges and zero-butyrate states limit claims based on a single pFBA point. Selected loopless endpoints additionally test whether internal cycles explain those ranges.

blocks.comment: Media files in the supplementary data: What is the derivation_factor?
blocks.response: The Methods define derivation_factor as the dimensionless multiplier in maxFlux = base_maxFlux * derivation_factor. It is a controlled perturbation of assumed model uptake capacity, not an empirical uptake measurement. The six-amino-acid multipliers derive from High-protein/EU-average AGORA ratios, whose dietary supply scale differs from the organism exchange-capacity scale.

blocks.comment: There is a folder marked benchmarking, with a PDF with a Supplementary Table S11 and a Supplementary Table S14 in addition to Supplementary Figure S2 which in the legend caption is called Figure 1. I do not see these referenced in the revised manuscript.
blocks.response: The active manuscript cites external benchmarking as S5-S6. The current consolidated supplementary index maps every S1-S73 identifier to explicit files and labels historical aliases. The immutable baseline benchmarking PDF retains the older S11/S14/S2 labels as historical provenance only; it is not an additional current supplement. Current S11 and S14 denote the carbon screen and production envelope, and the new sequence figure is Supplementary Figure S1. We state this distinction in the package README and supplementary index rather than silently renumbering the archived baseline.

blocks.comment: Figure 1B and D, and Figure 2A: There is some overlap of text in the figure.
blocks.response: Figures 1 and 2 have been regenerated with separated legends, titles and annotations. Figure 1C is now a table of nutrient-capacity multipliers, and Figure 1D is a descriptive three-condition bar comparison without a fitted trend. The growth-comparison annotation in Figure 2A has been moved outside the bar labels. The full compiled figures are rendered and visually checked before delivery. Figures 3-7 retain their already improved v4 image bytes; current captions are synchronized with the new results.

blocks.comment: Overall impression: The availability of the codes and comprehensive supplementary information and interesting simulation setups are the highlights of the manuscript. The model, however, requires curation of blocked reactions, GPR associations and biomass formulation.
blocks.response: Actual gene-rule curation and matched-strain controls now supplement the audit. Bcd/Rnf complex logic is corrected with sequence and neighborhood evidence, PFOR is annotated by full-length homology, and the numerical consequences for gene interventions and communities are tested. Remaining substrate specificity and target biomass measurements are explicit limits.

blocks.comment: The authors reconstruct a GEM of Megasphaera sp. MJR8396C and apply benchmarking, gutSMASH, nutrient perturbations, StrainDesign, and a two-member MICOM model with B. adolescentis. They conclude that the strain is nutrient-responsive and can act as a lactate-consuming butyrate producer. The reporting is candid and reproducible, but the central cross-feeding and strain-design conclusions rest on unvalidated or likely artifactual model behavior.
blocks.response: We agree with the central concern. The revised study no longer treats the archived high-butyrate reaction deletions as viable engineering designs or a feasible lactate exchange as evidence of necessary cross-feeding. Global GPR knockouts eliminate the attractive OK2-OK4 phenotypes, and donor-lactate-export blocking preserves the selected community growth states. The remaining conclusions concern constraint-dependent model behavior and robustness to explicit counterfactuals.

blocks.comment: 1. Methods 4.1 states that GCA_001546855.1 derives from a human vaginal isolate. The title, introduction, media, partner species (B. adolescentis), and obesity/fiber motivation are all gut-centered. This is never reconciled. Megasphaera is a well-known vaginal taxon, so the gut-like medium and bifidobacterial coculture may not reflect the strain's ecology. The supporting citations for the gut link (refs 55–56) are a fungal mycobiome pipeline (FunOMIC) and a renal-cell-carcinoma microbiota review. Neither obviously supports an association between this strain and fiber response or obesity. Ref 57 is the authors' own preprint. Please state the isolation site up front, justify the gut context with appropriate evidence (e.g., metagenomic detection of this strain in gut cohorts), or reframe the work as a generic Megasphaera model tested in gut-like conditions.
blocks.response: MJR8396C is now identified as a vaginal isolate at the start of the Abstract and Introduction and in the genome Methods. Gut-like media and the bifidobacterial partner are imposed model scenarios. We do not claim documented intestinal colonization, obesity association, fiber response or complex-carbohydrate degradation for this strain. The earlier inappropriate strain-specific citation argument is removed; related-strain physiology is identified explicitly as contextual evidence. The title describes a constraint-based analysis rather than an established gut ecological role.

blocks.comment: 2. Taxonomic placement is missing. The "sp." designation and comparisons with M. elsdenii, NM10, and BL7 rely on genus-level inference. The authors decline to compute ANI/dDDH or a GTDB placement (lines 213–214, 341–342, 555–556). This is a quick analysis, and it determines which reference strains are appropriate benchmarks. Genome size and GC for MJR8396C are also omitted from Fig. 3B, although both are trivially obtained from the assembly. Please add them.
blocks.response: Accession-matched sequence bytes were analyzed. Reciprocal skani/FastANI and both alignment fractions are supplied for DSM 20460, NM10, BL7 and closer reference genomes. skani ANI to the physiological comparators is 82.73-82.86%, with approximately 43-47% alignment fractions; it is not evidence of conspecificity. The exact assembly is assigned Megasphaera sp001546855 in GTDB R232, labelled as a release lookup rather than a newly run GTDB-Tk classification. Genome statistics are measured directly and plotted in Supplementary Figure S1: original JGI 2,426,262 bp/51.04337% GC and public assembly 2,453,897 bp/51.02898% canonical-base GC. The former comparative Figure 3 has been replaced by the current biomass/quality figure; the new sequence figure supplies the requested measurements without mixing assembly versions.

blocks.comment: 3. The lactate benchmark undermines the lactate-centered conclusions. The model predicts 0.156 h⁻¹ growth in the lactate-conditioned simulation against 0.62 h⁻¹ reported, a four-fold underprediction. It also predicts zero acetate, a 57% propionate fraction (vs. 35%), and a Jensen–Shannon distance of 0.52. The "13% above the published maximum" comparison pits a multi-substrate medium against a lactate-only culture, so it is not informative. The close butyrate match (11.33 vs. 10.4) is one point of agreement among several mismatches and may be coincidental. Yet the headline cross-feeding claim depends on exactly this lactate-oxidation capacity. Please diagnose the failure (CoA-transferase directionality, acrylate pathway stoichiometry, redox balance, NGAM, biomass template), state whether Bcd–Etf electron bifurcation is represented, which strongly affects ATP yield, and either curate the model or explicitly downgrade the conclusions that rely on lactate use.
blocks.response: Bcd-Etf bifurcation stoichiometry was already present and remains balanced. Its erroneous ETF-only OR GPR is now corrected to require catalytic Bcd and both ETF components. Complete Rnf and inferred PFOR gene rules are also added. These annotation edits leave wild-type fluxes unchanged, so they do not erase the lactate benchmark mismatch. Uptake/maintenance/biomass and unsupported-reaction sensitivities retain that uncertainty; the lactate-centered biological conclusion is downgraded.

blocks.comment: 4. Growth and flux predictions are largely set by arbitrary uptake bounds, and the reported growth rates are implausible. In Table 3, every supplied carbon source is consumed at its upper bound in every condition, so growth is bound-limited, not network-limited. Predicted rates of 0.70, 0.83, 1.20 (and 1.51 in MICOM) h⁻¹ exceed the highest published M. elsdenii rate (0.62 h⁻¹). The authors note the 1.2006 value is a "theoretical upper bound", but the paper still treats these numbers as outcomes (e.g., the "71% biomass increase"). The gut-like medium is also the one used for gapfilling, so growth is guaranteed by construction, and gapfill solutions are non-unique. I request a sensitivity analysis on uptake bounds, NGAM/GAM, and biomass template (which gapseq template was used for this diderm Negativicute is not stated), reporting of FVA ranges (not just pFBA points) for the Table 3 fluxes, since sulfur and nitrogen products are likely highly degenerate, an energy-generating-cycle check, and a loopless FVA or equivalent.
blocks.response: The original sensitivity and loop checks are extended with uniformly reconstructed exact-strain models, 432 new uptake/GAM/NGAM cases, 216 sequence-biomass/maintenance cases, ordinary FVA and 81 completed native fastSNP loopless FVA ranges. Template choice, gapfilling medium and nonunique reconstruction effects are explicit. Four AGORA formula-mass candidates, a common gross carbon budget and iME375 energy-cycle controls improve comparability. These are computational bounds, not experimentally calibrated growth rates.

blocks.comment:
5. The MICOM analysis appears confounded by medium scaling and is not shown to demonstrate cross-feeding.

MJR8396C grows at 1.5056 h⁻¹ in the community at tradeoff 1.0 versus 0.7005 h⁻¹ in monoculture. Table 5 shows total glucose uptake of 20.0 (16.35 + 3.65) and L-lactate of 20.0, i.e., exactly double the gut-like bounds. This suggests the medium bounds were applied per community gDW, so each member at 0.5 abundance effectively sees twice the nutrients. If so, the community and monoculture results are not comparable. Please clarify and renormalize.

Between tradeoff 0.95 and 1.0, MJR8396C growth changes from 0.715 to 1.506 h⁻¹ while B. adolescentis drops to zero. The "cooperative" state is sensitive to an arbitrary tradeoff choice and fixed 50:50 abundance. The two members' growth rates being nearly identical (0.715171 vs. 0.715175) suggests a regularization effect. Please provide abundance sensitivity and FVA or sampling of the exchange fluxes.

The paper never shows that MJR8396C grows faster or makes more butyrate in coculture than alone under identical effective constraints. Please compare against monoculture and include a transfer-blocked control (e.g., block B. adolescentis D-lactate secretion).
B. adolescentis takes up all 20 units of supplied L-lactate and apparently racemizes it to D-lactate (33.62 secreted, exceeding what 16.35 glucose could generate through the bifid shunt). Bifidobacteria are not typically net lactate consumers, and they usually produce mainly L-lactate. The "cross-feeding" may largely reflect the artificial L-lactate in the medium plus the model's lactate racemization. Please justify the stereochemistry with literature and test a medium without L-lactate.
blocks.response: An additional 1,920 native MICOM cases cover matched MJR8396C/NM10/BL7 models, sequence-curated sensitivities and original versus D-LDH-filtered 22L. Shared supplies are applied once per community biomass; taxon exchanges and growth are abundance weighted, with effective-supply monocultures and 4,320 exchange-FVA ranges. Removing unsupported 22L D-LDH eliminates D secretion without removing community growth. Direct comparisons retain four small growth benefits at 90% Megasphaera abundance with externally supplied lactate; all 116 feasible matched-growth monoculture butyrate intervals contain the community point. No-external-lactate and transfer-blocked controls do not establish lactate necessity. Equal selected member rates are attributed to regularization, not mutualism.

blocks.comment:
6. The StrainDesign results are probably dominated by model artifacts. OptKnock 2–4 pair deletions of GMP synthase (rxn00916) or CTP synthase (rxn00410) with lactate/acrylate-pathway steps. These nucleotide-biosynthesis reactions are essential in most bacteria, yet the model loses only about 5% growth. This suggests redundant or gapfilled bypass reactions, which makes the predicted +47% butyrate dubious. Please report the GPRs and gene counts for each target, check for isozyme or gapfill-derived bypasses, and test essentiality in a minimal-gapfill model.

OK2 and OK3 give identical phenotypes because they hit adjacent reactions in one pathway (rxn02123 and rxn90029). "Three strategies converged" overstates the independence.
The tilted-OptKnock objective is not defined in the Methods (weights, tilt parameters, constraints). Table 4 omits OK0/OK1, which are described in the text and Fig. 5 as butyrate-abolishing "OptKnock" designs, a confusing label for deletions that destroy the target phenotype.
No growth-coupling or yield-versus-growth analysis is shown to establish that the designs are actually growth-coupled.
blocks.response: The full historical settings and bounded search remain documented. The same chemical target sets and native global GPR implementations were tested in all new exact-strain models. All eighteen tested OK2-OK4 minimal gene implementations in MJR8396C, NM10 and BL7 have zero growth, despite viable reaction-only counterfactuals. Nucleotide target-gene essentiality is independently retained after GPR curation. Growth-product envelopes and missing-target/GPR cases are supplied. The interventions are not promoted as viable engineering designs or independent convergent strategies.

blocks.comment:
7. Stereospecific lactate partitioning (D→butyrate, L→propionate) is called "biologically plausible in light of lactate racemase" (lines 370–372). A functioning racemase would erase such partitioning, so the argument cuts the other way. Is racemase in the model? If not, this is likely an artifact of its absence.
The amino-acid set (Asp, Gly, Lys, Met, Cys, His) omits canonical Stickland donors (Leu/Ile/Val/Ala) and the main acceptor (Pro). Growth is also the only readout. The pair analysis cannot test the stated question. The interaction effects (≤0.00225 h⁻¹, <0.3% of growth) are too small to interpret as synergy or antagonism.
Amino-acid enrichment modifies only six amino acids, so "protein-rich" is an overgeneralization.
Doubling glucose cannot speak to fiber responses, and MJR8396C is not shown to degrade complex carbohydrates. The Discussion linking the results to the obesity and fiber literature (lines 428–442) goes beyond the evidence.
Acetate. In the carbon screen, acetate gives no growth gain (line 238), yet in Fig. 2D acetate raises growth and butyrate. These may be reconcilable (co-substrate and electron sink), but the mechanism should be shown.
blocks.response: The new matched panel tests all twenty amino acids and 190 pairs, including Leu/Ile/Val/Ala and Pro, with product fluxes alongside growth. This remedies the limited substrate panel without claiming biochemical Stickland coupling. No racemase is added solely to fit predictions: LarA-like matches and partial maturation evidence do not establish activity. Six-AA enrichment and glucose perturbation remain named precisely, acetate co-substrate mechanisms are retained, and fiber/obesity/clinical claims remain removed.

blocks.comment:
8. Table 2 reports "100% similarity" between Megasphaera and B. thetaiotaomicron PFOR II, and defines similarity as amino-acid identity. Identity of 100% across phyla is implausible. In antiSMASH-family tools the figure generally reflects the fraction of reference-cluster genes with homologs, not sequence identity. Please verify and correct the definition.
A 33% (Pdu) or 20% (4-aminobutyrate) hit is called "present", while 50% is "partial" in the text. Please apply and justify consistent criteria.
Methods 4.2 defines a concordant/partial/no-concordance scheme, but no concordance table appears in Results. Hypothesis (ii) is assessed only qualitatively. Please provide the table and the model fluxes through the Rnf and PFOR reactions per condition.
Chain elongation (valerate/caproate), a hallmark of the genus, is absent from the model. Please state whether this reflects gene absence or database limits.
blocks.response: Reference-cluster gene coverage remains distinct from amino-acid identity. The explicit concordance/flux tables are supplemented with sequence-supported Rnf, Bcd-Etf and PFOR GPR corrections. Original gutSMASH fractions are not used as activity evidence. Acrylate catalytic specificity, a complete Lar maturation system, Pdu/4-aminobutyrate route completeness and C5/C6 terminal chemistry remain qualified; no lack-of-gene claim follows from an absent model reaction.

blocks.comment: 9. There is no comparison with existing curated models. AGORA2 and the published M. elsdenii GEM (ref 50) are the obvious comparators. Comparing substrate utilization, product spectra, and lactate behavior against them, and against published phenotype data (ref 47), would show what is strain-specific rather than a generic gapseq outcome.
blocks.response: The deposited iME375 and six AGORA2 models now also have a common enriched-support/carbon-budget comparison with support sensitivity and FVA. Four positive, fully specified formula-mass biomass candidates are normalized separately; two generic-polymer cases remain unnormalizable. iME375 protein/DNA discrepancies are partially repaired, and an ATP cycle through reverse full CPS is identified and removed by a supported R421 direction constraint in separate candidates. Target measurements and unresolved polymer conventions still preclude a fully empirical absolute-growth ranking.

blocks.comment: The Discussion says amino-acid enrichment "reduced sulfur products", whereas Results, Table 3 (H₂S 1.93 ->4.57, MTTL 1.89->4.28), and the Abstract report an increase.
blocks.response: The current Results, Abstract and Discussion consistently report increased H2S and methanethiol in the selected-six-amino-acid-enriched pFBA state. We do not retain the contradictory reduced-sulfur claim. FVA uncertainty is described separately from the direction of the selected point comparison.

blocks.comment: Supplementary table numbering is inconsistent. Text cites S15–S17 for StrainDesign, the Fig. 5 caption cites S18–S19, and the Table 4 caption cites "Supplementary Tables 4a and 4b", while S4 is the non-GPR list.
blocks.response: The active StrainDesign discussion cites S41-S43 for deletion retests, gene-level effects and the new finite search, plus S53/S56 for native verification and recovered historical settings. Older S15-S19 files remain indexed as archived source tables. The current intervention-table and Figure 5 captions use the current identifiers and do not cite Supplementary Tables 4a/4b. One consolidated S1-S73 index records all canonical paths and historical aliases.

blocks.comment: There are literal "\n" strings in the axis labels of Fig. 1D, 4D, and 5A. The "0.700" label overlaps the annotation in Fig. 2A. Fig. 3C text is illegibly small. Fig. 1C is better as a table, and Fig. 1D has only three points.
blocks.response: Figures 1 and 2 are regenerated as described for Reviewer 1. Figure 1C is a multiplier table and panel D is a descriptive bar comparison. The revised Figures 3-7 use the previously improved layouts; their current captions and printed-size rendering are checked again. Literal backslash-n strings are not used as visible axis text. Numerical source values remain machine readable, while figure annotations are rounded for display.

blocks.comment: Growth rates such as 0.715171 h⁻¹ and fluxes to two decimals are unwarranted for a draft model.
blocks.response: Main-text physiological comparisons and tables use approximately three significant figures. More digits are retained only in machine-readable outputs and numerical solver-regression/residual checks, where they are needed for reproducibility and are not a claim of physiological precision.

blocks.comment: Explain why these six amino acids were chosen, and that the AA-rich multipliers (AGORA ratios, 1.8–2.3) come from a different scale than the model uptake capacities.
blocks.response: The six amino acids were inherited from the original defined gapfilling medium and perturbed while the other nutrients were held fixed. They were not selected as a complete dietary-protein or Stickland panel. The Methods specify all six dimensionless AGORA ratios and explain that dietary quantities and organism uptake capacities have different normalization scales.

blocks.comment: MEMOTE. The 37.3% gene-annotation score could be improved easily by adding UniProt/KEGG cross-references. Also report counts of mass- or charge-unbalanced reactions.
blocks.response: All 477 deposited genes now have sequence-supported public protein/locus mappings, and the annotation-only primary SBML adds NCBI protein cross-references and locus notes. We do not invent UniProt/KEGG functional assignments to improve a score. Historical MEMOTE is explicitly labelled and was not recomputed. Among assessable fully annotated internal reactions, the mass/charge audit detects zero imbalances; 195 MJR8396C and 147 partner internal reactions have incomplete/non-specific formulas and are reported separately. No unsupported proton-balance change was made.

blocks.comment: The authors have constructed a genome-scale metabolic model for Megasphaera sp. MJR8396C and have done flux balance simulations using different medium combinations of metabolites that mimic high-carbohydrate, amino acid-rich environments for the microbe to grow. They have assessed butyrate production by this species and simulated the model with Bifidobacterium adolescentis to verify potential cross-feeding, in which the Megasphaera model consumes lactate from Bifidobacterium and produces butyrate.
blocks.response: The current revision tests rather than assumes the proposed lactate mechanism. Native community controls show that the selected growth states persist after donor lactate-export blocking, and global gene deletions overturn the attractive reaction-only engineering interpretation. We report conditional exchange in an imposed nutrient setting and do not present the simulations as verification of the organisms in coculture.

blocks.comment: 1. An appropriate way to curate the metabolic model would have been to include the gutSMASH predicted pathways in the model as respective reactions and metabolites.
blocks.response: Core gutSMASH-associated chemistry already exists in the reconstruction; adding duplicate reactions would not curate it. We now correct the Bcd-Etf and six-subunit Rnf GPRs and add inferred PFOR associations using accession-resolved sequence and neighborhood evidence. Each edit is tested and separated from conservative bound sensitivities. Incomplete terminal or substrate-specific pathways are not invented from a cluster fraction; these remaining functional limits are explicit.

blocks.comment: 2. Because the manuscript emphasizes strain-level variation, the comparative analysis feels incomplete without evaluating the companion strains under identical conditions. To robustly substantiate claims of strain specificity, the authors should extend the full suite of in silico analyses, including medium simulations and cross-feeding evaluations with the Bifidobacterium model to both the NM10 and BL7 models, alongside MJR8396C. This will provide a true benchmark of phenotypic and metabolic divergence across strains.
blocks.response: New models of the exact NM10 and BL7 assemblies, plus new MJR8396C and 22L controls, have completed a uniform gapseq pipeline and matched media, carbon, twenty-AA/190-pair, maintenance, intervention, FVA/loopless and native-community analyses. The original published ModelSEED models were unavailable, so these are explicitly new reconstructions rather than claimed reproductions. Both raw and sequence-curated/conservative community suites are supplied. NM10 potential Bcd frameshift evidence is traced to the public annotation and treated as uncertainty.

blocks.comment: 3. The objective of some analysis in the study is unclear, If the goal of StrainDesign was to identify knockouts or interventions to maximize butyrate flux, how does this align with the findings from the community-level co-culture simulations, which demonstrate that Bifidobacterium adolescentis-derived lactate naturally drives elevated butyrate yields? From a bioprocess or metabolic engineering standpoint, could the authors explicitly discuss the comparative viability of an engineered monoculture versus a synthetic mutualistic co-culture? Clarifying the intended application will help unify these two distinct analyses.
blocks.response: The analyses now share an explicit question about robustness of production and exchange predictions under comparable constraints. Historical nucleotide-associated gene designs are nonviable in all three new Megasphaera models; lactate transfer is not necessary in the tested community controls. Neither calculation establishes superiority of engineered monoculture or a stable mutualistic consortium. Experimental productivity, yield and stability would be required to compare applications.

blocks.comment: 4. Can the authors also verify which particular strain of Bifidobacterium adolescentis was used here and whether that strain has the capability to produce D-lactate and consume L-lactate, based on some prior experimental work so that it verifies the flux results seen in the simulations?
blocks.response: The recovered source identifies B. adolescentis 22L, and all 349 deposited gene accession versions match its current accession-resolved proteins. A full-length L-LDH candidate has strong reviewed-reference support. The model D-LDH is an unassigned gapfill with no well-covered candidate in the limited panel. Disabling it in a separate sensitivity removes modeled D export while preserving selected community growth. The strain-specific primary fermentation assay measures total lactate; no enantiomer-resolved D secretion or net L uptake validation is claimed.

blocks.comment: 1. Fig.3 caption, “Genome size and GC content for MJR8396C are omitted where a uniformly processed value was not available in the analysis package”. What does this imply? Obviously, the genome size and GC content should be known for the strain; why can't that be plotted??
blocks.response: The unavailable-statistics wording is removed. Both original and public assembly length/GC were computed directly and plotted in Supplementary Figure S1. The original JGI assembly and public assembly are shown separately because their content and annotation differ despite every original contig mapping exactly to public sequence. The current Figure 3 instead presents biomass/quality diagnostics.

blocks.comment: 2. Page 13, under section 2.6, I think this text was for the older version of the manuscript; “Together, the two figures retain the biochemical interpretability of the original intervention analysis while replacing the former OptForce annotations with interventions computed using”
blocks.response: The unfinished sentence and old figure-history narration are absent from the current Results. We describe the actual archived deletion scenarios, global GPR retests and their implications. The clean/tracked pair is generated from one final source so the deleted historical sentence is not retained as current prose.

blocks.comment: 3. Also similar in section 4.10 page 27 “The original qualitative OptForce color coding was removed before overlaying the current StrainDesign targets.”
blocks.response: The old OptForce color-coding sentence is removed. The Methods now state the recovered StrainDesign tilt, candidate costs, constraints and provenance limits and distinguish that historical analysis from the newly specified finite enumeration and reduced-network sensitivity.

blocks.comment: 4. Text in the figures does not seem properly aligned, such as those in Fig 1D, 2A, 2C, 6B, 7D
blocks.response: Figures 1 and 2 are regenerated and their legends, annotations and table layout are inspected at the size used in the manuscript. The already improved Figures 3-7 are preserved and checked in the final rendered documents, including panels 6B and 7D. Figure captions distinguish archived independent-engine plots from the complete native MICOM validation; the obsolete claim that native MICOM was never run is removed.
